topic.name: Computing the Singular Values of a Matrix

question.text: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}?$
question.explanation:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} A^T \! A &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}^T \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 \\ -1 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 & -4 \\ -2 & -4 & 5 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} |A^T \! A - \lambda I| &= 0 \\[5pt] \begin{vmatrix} 4- \lambda & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4- \lambda & -4 \\ -2 & -4 & 5- \lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\[5pt] (4- \lambda) \begin{vmatrix} 4- \lambda & -4 \\ -4 & 5- \lambda \end{vmatrix} - 2 \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 4- \lambda \\ -2 & -4 \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\[5pt] (4- \lambda) \big( (4- \lambda)(5- \lambda) - 16 \big) - 4 (4- \lambda) &= 0 \\[5pt] (4- \lambda) \big( 20 - 4\lambda - 5\lambda + \lambda^2 - 16 \big) - 4 (4- \lambda) &= 0 \\[5pt] (4- \lambda) \big( \lambda^2 - 9\lambda + 4 \big) - 4 (4- \lambda) &= 0 \\[5pt] (4- \lambda) (\lambda^2 - 9\lambda + 4 - 4) &= 0 \\[5pt] (4- \lambda) (\lambda^2 - 9\lambda) &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda(\lambda - 4) (\lambda - 9) &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda &= 9, \, 4, \: 0 \end{align*}

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

\begin{align*} \sigma_1 &= \sqrt{\lambda_1} = \sqrt{9} = 3 \\[3pt] \sigma_2 &= \sqrt{\lambda_2} = \sqrt{4} = 2 \\[3pt] \sigma_3 &= \sqrt{\lambda_3} = \sqrt{0} = 0 \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Singular Values of a Square Matrix

question.text:
Which of the following statements are true?

  1. The matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix} -10 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ has one negative singular value.
  2. Any $2\times4$ matrix $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.
  3. Any $6\times3$ matrix $A$ has at most $6$ distinct singular values.
question.explanation:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ can't have any negative singular value.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $2 \times 4$ matrix and $A^T$ is a $4\times 2$ matrix, $A^T \! A$ must be a $4 \times 4$ matrix: \[ \underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4} \times {\large 2}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 2} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4}}{A} = \underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 4}}{A^T \! A} \] Hence, $A$ has at most $4$ distinct singular values.

  • Statement III is false. Since $A$ is a $6 \times 3$ matrix and $A^T$ is a $3\times 6$ matrix, $A^T \! A$ must be a $3 \times 3$ matrix: \[ \underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 3} \times {\large 6}}{A^T} \times \underset{{\large 6} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 3}}{A} = \underset{\bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 3} \times \bbox[Gainsboro, 2pt]{\large 3}}{A^T \! A} \] Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

example.title: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Singular Values of a Matrix

question.text: What are the singular values of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1& 0\\ 0&-2& 0 \end{bmatrix}?$
question.explanation:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T \! A.$

First, we calculate $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} A^T \! A &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1& 0\\ 0&-2& 0 \end{bmatrix}^T \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1& 0\\ 0&-2& 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1& 0\\ 0&-2& 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} |A^T \! A - \lambda I| &= 0 \\[5pt] \begin{vmatrix} 8 - \lambda & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 5 - \lambda & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0- \lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\[5pt] (- \lambda) \begin{vmatrix} 8- \lambda & 2 \\ 2 & 5- \lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\[5pt] (- \lambda) \big( (8- \lambda)(5- \lambda) - 4 \big) &= 0 \\[5pt] (-\lambda) (\lambda^2 - 13\lambda+36) &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda(\lambda - 4) (\lambda - 9) &= 0 \\[5pt] \lambda &= 9, \, 4, \: 0 \end{align*}

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

\begin{align*} \sigma_1 &= \sqrt{\lambda_1} = \sqrt{9} = 3 \\[3pt] \sigma_2 &= \sqrt{\lambda_2} = \sqrt{4} = 2 \\[3pt] \sigma_3 &= \sqrt{\lambda_3} = \sqrt{0} = 0 \end{align*}
